props.title: Inland Empire
props.initialSlug: An actress loses herself in a cursed film role

sections.content: Inland Empire represents David Lynch's most experimental and challenging work, pushing digital video to surreal extremes. Shot over several years on consumer-grade DV cameras, the film follows Laura Dern's splintering performance as an actress whose identity fractures during a cursed film production. Unlike the more narratively grounded Mulholland Drive (2001), Inland Empire deliberately destroys conventional storytelling, creating a three-hour nightmare landscape where Polish folk tales, sitcom rabbits, and Hollywood degradation collide. The low-fi digital imagery creates an unsettling intimacy, with Lynch using the medium's limitations to heighten the psychological horror.

sections.content: The film builds on Lynch's career-long exploration of fractured identity and Hollywood's dark underbelly. While Blue Velvet (1986) and Lost Highway (1997) maintained some narrative coherence, Inland Empire completely abandons traditional structure. It shares DNA with experimental works like Meshes of the Afternoon (1943) and Last Year at Marienbad (1961), films that prioritize dream logic and psychological states over plot. The digital video creates a uniquely unsettling texture, predating the found footage horror boom of films like Paranormal Activity (2007). SUBHEAD: Digital Experimentation and Performance

Laura Dern's fearless performance anchors the experimental chaos. Her character Nikki Grace/Susan Blue exists in multiple realities, echoing the dual roles of Persona (1966) and That Obscure Object of Desire (1977). The digital intimacy allows Lynch to capture every microexpression as identity dissolves. This approach influenced later digital experimentalists like Shane Carruth's Upstream Color (2013) and Jonathan Glazer's Under the Skin (2013), though few dare to push as far into abstraction as Lynch.
